title: Arjuna Stands Up
hookLine: eighteen chapters later, Arjuna's confusion is gone, and the week comes back
carry: karma yoga: act fully, offer the fruit
tomorrow: why is there a stick in the middle of Nani's line?
last: READ IT YOURSELF, AND WITH SOMEONE.

cards: Eighteen chapters after his bow slipped from his hand, Arjuna is still in the chariot between two armies, with Krishna holding the reins. Krishna has finished teaching.
And he asks one last question: have you heard all this with a focused mind? Is your confusion gone?

teach.b: Arjuna answers: my confusion is gone. By your grace I remember. My doubts have fallen away.
I will do as you say. The Gita ends there; the epic goes on, and Arjuna fights. Walk back through the week and you can see what changed him.
Day one, karma yoga: his right is to the action, never to its fruits. Then Maitreyi, turning down a fortune to ask about the atman, the Self that makes anything dear.
Then shruti: holy words heard first, written later, Ganesha holding the pen for Vyasa.

Then Shabari's tasted berries and bhakti: offer the fruit with love, and God accepts it. Then abhyasa, the restless mind held by coming back, bead by bead. Then svadhyaya: study with someone who has lived inside it.
Put together, it's one way of life: act fully, offer what comes of it, know who you really are, keep coming back, and learn it from someone.
Priya's card sits on her desk with half of Nani's line inside: karmany evadhikaras te, ma phaleshu kadachana. Your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits.
Even the marks hold the week: the knot in karma, the curl in adhi, the e and the u of phaleshu. A week ago it was squiggles. Now she knows she isn't writing it to make Nani cry.
She's writing it as an offering. What Nani does with it is the fruit.

how: Students often learn a Gita verse by copying it out by hand and reciting it with a teacher, half a line at a time, until it can be said from memory; many temples and families recite the Gita together on Gita Jayanti.

o: a word for the fruits of action
the script of Nani's line from the Gita

games.q: the week in one chariot — tap the pairs.
p: sets down his bow: I will not fight
my confusion is gone; I'll do as you say

s: at the end of the Gita, Arjuna still refuses to fight
he says his confusion is gone and he'll do as Krishna says.
Nani's line and Krishna's leaf-flower-fruit line use the same word for fruit
phala: don't cling to the fruit; offer it.
karma yoga means giving up action
it means acting fully and offering the fruit.

games.q: a friend says the Gita's message is 'don't care about results, just chill'. using the week, what's a better summary?
o: act fully, offer the fruit to God, keep coming back, and learn it from someone who lives it.
it's only advice for soldiers in battle.
games.why: karma yoga isn't not caring. Arjuna gets up and acts, the fruit offered, his confusion gone.

practice: Say the half line aloud, slowly, one piece per breath out: karmany, evadhikaras te, ma phaleshu, kadachana. Don't worry about getting it perfect. Then bring to mind whatever you'll do next.
If you pray, offer it now, before you begin; if you don't, simply hold it lightly, without its fruit. Sit in the quiet after.

wordCard.voice: Devanagari, once more: the script of Nani's line, and a week of teachings in half a line of it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ever, at any time; in the Gita's line, 'never' with ma.

carryVoice: For the road: karma yoga. Act fully, offer the fruit, let it go. A week, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.47, first half (karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana)
